transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-25
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Alex Turner (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Tom Alvarez (CTO - Sunnyside Health), Maya Chen (Head of ML), Jordan Lee (Product)
Link to deck: https://app.redwood.ai/decks/rate-limits (shared)
Security doc link: https://redwood.ai/security/soc2.pdf

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, uh, thanks for taking the time. I'm Alex, I'm the AE on this account, and with me is Priya from our solutions engineering team. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Tom: Good, thanks. Getting a quick coffee. Excited to see the org and project key flow — we got a couple questions on billing separation.
[00:12] Maya: Yeah primarily: can we have per-team quotas, and maintain per-project billing lines so finance can charge back?
[00:18] Priya: Totally. We'll go through the Console first, show org/project keys, then demo rate limits, quotas, and how Redwood handles burst and fallback routing. Also touch on Dedicated vs Hosted for multitenant constraints.
[00:29] Jordan: Great. Also, on security, Tom wants to know about SSO and KMS integration — and we have some residency requirements.
[00:35] Alex: Yup, we have a security appendix and the SOC2 doc (link above). We support SAML SSO, RBAC at org and project levels, and KMS/HSM integrations for Private deployments. For hosted, we offer customer-managed KMS for key wrapping if needed — details in the security docs.
[00:50] Priya: Ok jumping into the Console. (screen share) You can see on the left the org hierarchy. We create an org, then projects underneath. Each project gets a project key and optional rate policy.
[01:05] Priya: If I click Projects -> "Rx-Frontend", you can see quota windows: daily token quota, monthly contract quota, and a hard rate limit for requests per second. These are configurable per project or inherited from org defaults.
[01:22] Tom: If we set a daily token quota on the project, does that strictly stop requests or queue them?
[01:27] Priya: Good question. You can choose the enforcement mode: hard reject, soft limit with notification, or throttle with exponential backoff. Hard reject returns 429 and a suggestion header. Soft limit logs and alerts in Console but allows overage for a window. Throttle applies smoothing at the gateway.
[01:45] Maya: For our cost control, we probably want to hard cap per-project and then allow a separate overflow project for burst staging. Can we route overflow automatically?
[01:53] Priya: Yes — Redwood supports routing policies. You can set a fallback route that sends overflow requests to a cheaper model or a dedicated capacity pool. For example, if project A hits daily quota, route to a lower-cost quantized model or to a retry policy that returns cached results (prefix/KV cache).
[02:11] Jordan: You mentioned KV cache — is that per project or shared? We've had noisy neighbors in other systems.
[02:18] Priya: Cache can be scoped per project or shared at org level. For multi-tenant isolation we recommend per-project caches. There's also automatic prefix caching in the runtime which you can whitelist for shared caches.
[02:31] Alex: Quick note: some transcripts / docs sometimes say k v cache — but it's the same thing, we've seen transcription glitches before.
[02:38] Tom: (laughs) That makes sense. On the billing side, how do we do chargebacks? We want usage by project, broken down by token type (prompt vs completion) and per-route.
[02:49] Priya: The Console provides token-level billing breakdowns per project and per route. You can export daily CSVs and integrate with your billing system via webhook. We also have an API endpoint to pull usage programmatically.
[03:05] Maya: Can we set quotas that apply to a set of projects (e.g., a team) rather than single project?
[03:11] Priya: Yes, you can set pool quotas at the org or team level. Projects inherit defaults but you can override at project granularity. We also support project tags and label-based policies for policy-as-code.
[03:24] Jordan: Signup flows — how do we provision project keys for developers? We want self-serve but with guardrails so devs can't spin up huge budgets.
[03:32] Alex: You can enable auto-provisioning with quota templates. For example, all new projects get a starter quota of X tokens/day and require owner approval for higher limits. The org admins can set limits on who can request higher quotas.
[03:44] Tom: Let's talk latency. If we use Dedicated, do we still have rate limits enforced at the routing layer?
[03:51] Priya: Yes — Dedicated has local rate enforcement but the control plane configures the policies. Dedicated pools can be pinned to certain models and offer predictable throughput. If Dedicated pool saturates, we support graceful fallback to hosted instances if policy allows. For strict isolation and data residency, you can run Private with a customer-managed control plane.
[04:13] Maya: On Private, can we use our HSM/KMS?
[04:16] Alex: Yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and we provide documentation for key wrapping and rotation. For Hosted, we offer an option to integrate your KMS for encryption at rest and in transit.
[04:28] Tom: Are there any gotchas for bursty patterns? We occasionally have spiky traffic 2–3x baseline for a few minutes when marketing links are sent out.
[04:36] Priya: There are two knobs — burst allowance and burst windows. You can allow short-term bursts above the steady-state rate (we call it token bucket parameters) and configure autoscaling thresholds. For longer bursts, you might want a dedicated burst pool or a route to a cheaper model. We can demo autotuning suggestions from Redwood Optimize that look at historical traffic and recommend bucket sizes.
[04:59] Jordan: How do per-route limits work with function/tool calls? For us, some routes are expensive because they call a retriever + generator.
[05:07] Priya: You can define per-route cost weights. The Console lets you set a weight multiplier so a retriever+generator combo counts as X tokens or Y units. That feeds into quota enforcement and billing. We also support custom metrics for scoring cost so your observability can align with billing.
[05:25] Tom: Regarding retry logic, if a request is 429, do you recommend client side backoff or server side queuing?
[05:31] Priya: Both. Client-side exponential backoff is standard; server-side you can set a small queue with priority for important routes and graceful degradation for less critical flows. We provide sticky headers in the response to indicate retry-after and suggested backoff.
[05:47] Maya: Have you integrated with our identity provider? We use Okta and want SAML for the Console.
[05:53] Alex: Yes Okta via SAML is supported, plus SCIM for user provisioning. We can share a step-by-step guide.
[06:00] Jordan: Any limits on number of projects? We plan to spin up projects per customer tenant — hundreds maybe.
[06:06] Priya: We support large orgs and thousands of projects; performance scales. There are practical quotas for metadata calls (API rate limits) but projects themselves are first-class. For very large scale we recommend using our org-level routing and tags to manage groups of projects.
[06:20] Tom: Session got a little tech — can we run a quick POC? We want Redwood to run our prompt set through a dedicated pool and show latency/throughput and cost per 1M tokens.
[06:29] Alex: Absolutely — that's aligned with our pilot offering. We'll stand up a dedicated pool, run your prompts, and produce a benchmark sheet with p50/p95 latency and token costs. Priya will run the tests.
[06:38] Priya: I'll need a sample prompt set and an API key with a test project. Jordan, can you share a small set (50–200 prompts) and expected concurrency?
[06:45] Jordan: Yes I'll put that in a shared folder — aim for 200 concurrent requests to emulate peak.
[06:50] Maya: Also include prompts that are expensive — multi-step calls.
[06:55] Priya: Great. For the benchmark I'll run three configs: Hosted highest-performance model, Dedicated with 4-GPU pool, and Dedicated quantized model for cost-optimized baseline. I'll measure p50/p95 token latency and throughput, and report cost per 1M tokens.
[07:12] Alex: Next on routes — we talked about fallback policies. If we fall back to a quantized model, how do we handle quality regression alerts?
[07:20] Priya: Redwood Optimize can tie quality checks to prompt sets and send regression alerts. You can set canaries and automatic rollback if quality drops past a threshold. Those alerts are surfaced in Console and via webhooks.
[07:32] Tom: For compliance, we'd prefer all logs to be view-only and only stored for 90 days. Can we set retention per org or project?
[07:40] Priya: Yes retention is configurable per org/project. For Private or Dedicated with extended retention we offer add-on retention packages. You can also export logs to your SIEM.
[07:52] Jordan: How about throttling webhooks? If we hit the quota for webhooks we don't want retries to blow up our systems.
[07:58] Priya: We support dead letter queues and webhook rate limiting. Clients can set backoff. We also recommend fan-out with a managed delivery queue to protect your endpoints.
[08:10] Tom: Any integration work on our side for keys? We want to use project keys in the app so devs can use them but they expire after 30 days and need rotation.
[08:17] Alex: Project keys support TTLs and automatic rotation. You can also bind keys to IP ranges and VPCs for extra security. For CI we recommend using short-lived tokens minted via the org auth service.
[08:30] Maya: A quick nit — we've seen vendor docs that confuse organization / project naming, will this be clean in APIs?
[08:36] Priya: API is pretty explicit: org_id and project_id are required in calls that need scoping. We also provide client SDKs that set project context so it's easier for devs. There can be transcription errors in call notes where it becomes org.project vs org/project but API is explicit.
[08:50] Alex: We're about halfway through — want to switch to a quick live demo of policy creation?
[08:55] Tom: Yeah let's do that.
[09:00] Priya: (screenshare) Creating a new rate policy: name, window, tokens, enforcement. I'll create "marketing-burst" with a 5-minute window, 3x burst allowance, and fallback to "overflow-quant" model.
[09:18] Priya: Save. Now I'll attach it to the "marketing" project. You can test it via the API: POST /v1/projects/{project_id}/execute with project key header.
[09:28] Jordan: If a request is routed to overflow-quant, do logs show the original project ID? We need traceability for billing.
[09:34] Priya: Yes we preserve original project_id and add routing metadata. Billing is still attributed to the original project unless you specifically route billing to a different project for overage accounting.
[09:45] Tom: That's good. We want finance to see where the overage happened and decide whether to bill dev teams or central ops.
[09:52] Alex: That can be configured; you can have overage billed to a central "ops" project.
[09:58] Maya: Do rate limits apply to embeddings differently? We use embeddings heavily and want different quotas.
[10:04] Priya: You can define quotas by API surface: text-gen, chat, embeddings. Each has separate counters and you can convert cost to a normalized unit for cross-surface quotas.
[10:16] Jordan: For the pilot, we'll probably start with dedicated for the production-like traffic and hosted for dev/staging.
[10:22] Alex: Sounds reasonable. We'll include a suggested org config for that split.
[10:27] Tom: Anything else on security? Encryption at rest, in transit, key rotation?
[10:32] Priya: All supported. For Private we recommend customer KMS. For Hosted we can integrate your KMS for key wrapping. Rotation supported via API, and we keep audit logs of key usage.
[10:45] Maya: How do you surface tokenized usage to our SIEM?
[10:49] Alex: Logs can be streamed to your SIEM via secure delivery; we support AWS Kinesis, GCP Pub/Sub, and custom webhooks.
[10:56] Jordan: Ok good. We need the pricing so procurement can review next week.
[11:00] Alex: I'll send the pricing deck and the dedicated capacity estimator.
[11:05] Priya: I'll follow up with the benchmark plan and a short runbook for setting up project keys and SSO.
[11:12] Tom: Thanks, useful session. Quick question — do you have any competitor tradeoffs to note?
[11:16] Alex: Compared to managed endpoints from cloud providers, Redwood focuses on developer ergonomics for multi-tenant control and cost levers. Compared to pure self-hosted runtimes, we provide unified console, billing, and Optimize recommendations so you don't build all the tooling. Some customers use a hybrid.
[11:33] Jordan: Good. Let's wrap with next steps.
[11:36] Alex: Recap of next steps: Alex sends pricing and org/project guide; Priya runs benchmarks and shares results; Jordan provides prompt set and concurrency target; Maya provides compliance checklist. We'll aim to kick off pilot week of 2025-07-07.
[11:50] Tom: Sounds good. Thanks all.
[11:52] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with the scheduling link.
